sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: At senior and staff level, interviewers move from language syntax to runtime behaviour because production incidents at scale are almost always about memory pressure, GC pauses, goroutine leaks, or CPU contention. Understanding how the Go runtime allocates memory, what the tri-color GC does, and how to use pprof to investigate issues signals that you can own performance-critical services, not just write correct ones.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: Go's runtime manages two allocation arenas: the stack (per-goroutine, grows/shrinks automatically, very cheap) and the heap (shared, GC-managed, more expensive). Escape analysis is the compiler pass that decides which allocations go to the stack vs the heap — a value 'escapes' to the heap when its lifetime must outlive the stack frame. The GC is a concurrent tri-color mark-sweep: it classifies objects as white (not yet seen), grey (reachable but not fully scanned), and black (fully scanned), running most work concurrently with the application to minimise stop-the-world pauses. GOGC controls the heap growth trigger ratio; GOMAXPROCS controls OS-thread parallelism.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
• Stack vs heap: stack allocations are free (pointer bump); heap allocations require GC tracking.
• Escape analysis: use go build -gcflags='-m' to see what escapes and why; closures capturing a local variable cause escapes.
• Tri-color mark-sweep: concurrent mark phase + short STW at start/end; write barrier maintains invariant during concurrent marking.
• GOGC: default 100 means GC triggers when heap doubles since last collection; lower = more frequent GC, less peak memory; higher = less GC, more memory.
• pprof: go tool pprof for heap (alloc_objects, inuse_objects), CPU profiles, and goroutine dumps; http/pprof endpoint for live services.
• Race detector: go run/test -race; instruments memory accesses at runtime; ~5–10x slowdown, use in CI not production.
• GOMAXPROCS: defaults to number of logical CPUs; setting it lower can reduce scheduler contention in mixed workloads.
• Benchmarking: testing.B with b.N; use -benchmem for allocation counts; -count=5 for statistical stability.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
• 'How does Go decide whether to allocate on the stack or heap?' — escape analysis at compile time.
• 'What is GOGC and how would you tune it for a latency-sensitive service?' — lower GOGC reduces pause times at the cost of more frequent collections.
• 'Describe the tri-color mark-sweep algorithm.' — white/grey/black classification, concurrent mark, write barrier, short STW.
• 'How would you diagnose a memory leak in a running Go service?' — pprof heap profile via /debug/pprof/heap, compare inuse_objects over time.
• 'What does the race detector do and when would you run it?' — instruments memory accesses, reports concurrent unsynchronised reads/writes; run in CI/test, not in production.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "When a Go service starts showing elevated latency or growing memory, my first stop is pprof. I expose the net/http/pprof endpoint in staging and capture a heap profile before and after a load test to see which allocation sites are growing. For GC-related latency spikes I look at the GC trace output and consider lowering GOGC, which trades peak memory for more frequent but shorter collection cycles. On the compiler side I use -gcflags='-m' to spot unexpected escapes — things like a local struct being passed to an interface parameter will escape to the heap and add GC pressure in hot paths. For concurrency bugs I always run the race detector in CI; it catches data races that would be nearly impossible to reproduce manually. I think of GOMAXPROCS as something to leave at the default unless profiling shows scheduler overhead, which usually only matters in very mixed CPU/IO workloads."
